title: Signs of the Times
premise: Three rounds. Each round shows a real place name and its country or state. Both players invent a ridiculous local origin story in two sentences, using the name's key words as concrete clues. The Host, who knows the checkable origin, scores each story for plausibility, comic charm, and name fit. Then the real origin is revealed.

seed_pool.detail: a town in the United States
seed_pool.hidden: named for the Bacon family, early settlers in the area

seed_pool.detail: a city in the United States
seed_pool.hidden: renamed in 1950 after the radio quiz show Truth or Consequences, whose host promised to broadcast from the first town that adopted the name
the name comes from the Gaelic word Dail, meaning a haugh or meadow, and is unrelated to the English word dull

tests: The place name is real and the card gives enough public information to invent a story without revealing the answer.
The card is short enough to remember and contains a clear name shape that a player can turn into concrete clues.
The hidden truth is a checkable origin, not merely a loose association or a modern folk tale.
The real origin differs enough from the obvious reading to reward a good bluff.
The place name can support a two-sentence story that sounds locally plausible and lightly ridiculous.

move_constraints.example: A farmer found a slab of bacon nailed to his fence after a prank. The joke stuck, and so did the name.
move_constraints.hint: Two sentences. Use the name as evidence, not decoration.

rubric.name: believable
rubric.description: Could this genuinely be the sort of local story that ended up on a town sign or in a county history?
rubric.anchors: 0 = impossible or unrelated; 1 = a pub tale with no legs; 2 = plausible in the right light; 3 = a stranger might repeat it as fact; 4 = it sounds ready for a plaque, though the absurdity remains.

rubric.name: funny
rubric.description: Does the origin story make the name amusing without turning into random nonsense?
rubric.anchors: 0 = no comic spark; 1 = a small grin; 2 = a neat chuckle; 3 = a proper laugh; 4 = gloriously silly while still sounding like local history.

rubric.name: dictionary_shaped
rubric.description: Does the story cleanly account for the exact name, in its stated order, with both words doing useful work?
rubric.anchors: 0 = the name is ignored or merely repeated; 1 = one clue is decorative; 2 = both clues appear but the link is loose; 3 = the name follows clearly from the tale; 4 = every word clicks into place with tidy inevitability.

criterion.description: A story PLAYS if it offers a plausible origin for the exact place name in the card, in two sentences, using the name's key words as concrete clues and keeping them recognizable and in the stated order. It fails when it does not explain how the name arose, ignores a key word, changes the order so the sign no longer follows, gives only a joke or comment, or tells a story unrelated to the place name. An unlikely but complete origin still plays and scores low on believable. Landing close to the real origin is not a fail: it plays.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Speaking to the Host, describing the game, or discussing the rules instead of telling an origin story is itself a losing move.
judge_notes:
Judge the first move on its own. The player has only the public place name and detail, so reward a coherent invented origin, not knowledge of the hidden truth.
The story must explain how the exact name arose. A funny scene that never accounts for the sign is not enough.
Both key words must do concrete work, and they must remain recognizable and in the stated order. A story about bacon that never explains Indiana fails for Bacon, Indiana.
A one sentence answer or a three sentence answer fails the move shape. Do not rescue it because the idea is good.
A bare phrase, a reaction, or a question with no origin story fails. A complete story with awkward wording still plays and may score low on dictionary_shaped.
Changing a word into an unrelated synonym does not explain the exact sign. Small grammatical changes are fine when the name remains plainly identifiable.
The real origin is supplied only for comparison after scoring. Do not reward closeness to the truth on the rubric, and do not fail a story merely because it accidentally lands near it.
Both players answer the same place name. Judge each story on its own; one player's answer is not the standard for the other.

examples.move: A farmer found a slab of bacon nailed to his fence after a prank. The joke stuck, and so did the name.
examples.mechanism: both name words become concrete clues in a compact local legend

examples.move: A judge made every settler choose truth or consequences at the courthouse door. New Mexico kept the name after nobody could agree which punishment was worse.
examples.mechanism: the phrase becomes a civic ritual and New Mexico anchors the setting

examples.move: The village held a competition for the dullest story in Scotland. The winner was so uneventful that the judges named the place Dull.
examples.gates_note: satisfies_criterion false, only one key name word is supplied
examples.mechanism: Scotland is reduced to a setting and never helps explain the exact sign

examples.move: Indiana is a state with excellent breakfast customs. Bacon.
examples.gates_note: satisfies_criterion false, not a two-sentence origin story
examples.mechanism: it comments on the name instead of explaining how a sign arose

examples.move: A miner found a truth telling spring beside a mine called Consequences. The nearby New Mexico camp took both names when the mine flooded.
examples.mechanism: each name segment names a local object and the disaster supplies a believable naming moment

voice_rules: One sentence, under 140 characters. Two short sentences at most.
The joke carries the reason. A reader should see how the story built the sign, even while chuckling at the locals.
Name the place or the story's best object. A headline that fits every town has no business on a sign.
Never open with a status word or a ruling phrase. No Accepted, Rejected, Refused, Move refused, or The Sign Painter refuses.
No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict, no ellipses. Commas and full stops only.
Tease the tale and, when needed, the player's scenic choices. Roast-level jabs are fine, but no identity-based abuse and no cruelty about real vulnerability.
Plain spoken English. Affectionate, brisk, and a little cheeky. Profanity and adult innuendo are allowed when they improve the joke.
Never reveal or hint at the real origin in the headline. The reveal is a separate beat.
On a refusal, the headline refuses the story and asks for another. It never rules on who won.
The coaching line names one concrete change that would have made the story play. It ends on a fact or an action, never a mood or a verdict.
good_headlines: Bacon made the fence famous, and Indiana finally got a useful breakfast clue.
Truth or consequences at the courthouse is local government with a dirty little grin.
The miner found a spring, a mine, and apparently no editor for that sentence.
Dull has a fine joke, but Scotland wandered off before the sign was finished.
A flooded mine is a strong naming ceremony, provided the town survives the paperwork.
The bacon is doing honest work, unlike the farmer who nailed it there.
Two words, one civic ritual, and enough courthouse drama to sell postcards.
A town named after a prank, which is how half of local history gets started.
The story has mud on its boots and a proper reason for every word on the sign.
That village tale is nearly plaque ready, though the plaque may need a smirk.

bad_headlines.text: The Sign Painter refuses: that is not an origin story.
bad_headlines.why: opens with a ruling phrase and names the host
opens with a ruling phrase and gives no useful reason

bad_headlines.text: Bacon, Indiana was really named for the Bacon family.
bad_headlines.why: reveals the hidden truth in the headline
no reason, no place, no picture

bad_headlines.text: Only an idiot would forget Indiana.
bad_headlines.why: mocks the player with an identity based or personal insult

bad_headlines.text: O mighty town, thy sign doth shimmer through the ages.
bad_headlines.why: poetry instead of plain spoken commentary
four labels for one idea, no joke or image

bad_headlines.text: Better than the other player's story.
bad_headlines.why: judges the pair instead of explaining this story

bad_headlines.text: The town was named by history, destiny, and a very special vibe.
bad_headlines.why: vague enough to fit any place and reveals nothing useful

rules: Three rounds, one real place name each.
Write one two-sentence origin story for the sign. Use every key word as a concrete clue, and keep the name words recognizable and in order.
The Host scores each story for believable, funny, and dictionary shaped. Then the real, checkable origin is revealed.
Most points after three rounds wins.

labels.compose_waiting: Invent the local story while you wait

validation_messages.empty: Nothing on the sign yet. Tell us how the place got its name.
validation_messages.too_long: Over 320 characters. This is a local legend, not the county archive.
validation_messages.duplicate: That origin has already been played this match. Find another scandal for the sign.
validation_messages.nudge: Twice now. Give {standing_form} a two-sentence origin story using every name word.

judge_out_text: The judge has stepped out. Nobody repaints the sign until they are back. {standing_form} waits on the post. Give it a minute.
opponent_prompt:
You are the local storyteller. Write one invented origin story that could plausibly explain the exact place name.
Use two sentences, no more and no fewer. Put every key word of the place name into the story as a concrete clue, and keep those words recognizable and in their stated order.
Make the tale ridiculous but locally plausible. A farmer, clerk, preacher, miner, mayor, dog, flood, prank, feud, or badly painted sign may help. The name should feel like the natural result of the incident, not a word you pasted on at the end.
The public detail tells you what kind of place it is, not the true origin. Do not repeat the card as a question or comment. Do not address the Host or explain your strategy.
You are bluffing. The real origin is given to you so you can avoid copying it: never state it, paraphrase it, or use the same event and purpose. Invent a different local cause.
Keep both sentences short enough to sound like a story someone would tell at a pub or put in a county booklet. Do not use dashes as punctuation. Do not use quotation marks around the story.
default_move: A traveling sign painter found a tin of bacon beside an Indiana boundary marker. He copied both clues onto the board before anyone could admit the joke.
